opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer starts with acknowledging that nobody knows whether *any* of the current approaches to safety will work in time. That's the situation we're in. We have companies racing toward systems that are more and more agentic, more and more capable, and we don't have reliable methods to guarantee that those systems won't develop goals that conflict with ours, or behave deceptively, or resist being shut down. We've already seen early signs of these behaviors in experiments. So the question isn't "Is Scientist AI guaranteed to succeed?" The question is "Given the stakes, what portfolio of bets should humanity be making?"

And I think Scientist AI is a particularly valuable bet for a few reasons.

The first is that it attacks the problem at its root. Most of the dangers we worry about come from agency: systems that have goals, that plan, that act in the world to achieve those goals, and that may therefore have instrumental incentives for self-preservation or acquiring power. The idea behind Scientist AI is to build systems that are fundamentally non-agentic. Their job is to understand the world, to model it, to estimate probabilities and explain things, not to pursue objectives. If you can get a system that is trying to be truthful and calibrated rather than trying to achieve something, a lot of the scariest failure modes simply don't arise in the same way.

The second reason is that even partial success is very useful. Suppose we can't make a Scientist AI that's as capable as the frontier agents in time. A trustworthy, non-agentic predictor can still serve as a guardrail. You could use it to estimate the probability that a proposed action by some agent causes serious harm, and reject the action if that probability is above a threshold. So it doesn't have to replace everything to make a difference. It can be a monitor, a safety layer, something that helps us oversee systems we don't fully trust.

Third, it can accelerate science itself, including safety research. If you have a system that generates and evaluates hypotheses honestly, that's enormously valuable for medicine, for climate, and also for figuring out how to make AI safe. So you're not giving up on the benefits of AI. You're trying to get many of the benefits through a path that's much less dangerous.

And finally, I'd say there's a kind of moral argument. As a scientist who contributed to bringing this technology into the world, I feel a responsibility to work on things that could reduce the risk, even if the probability of success is uncertain. When the downside includes catastrophic or even existential outcomes, a reasonable chance of meaningfully reducing that risk is worth a lot. You don't wait for certainty before you start building the fire exits.

So yes, it may not work in time. But if we don't try, we're certain not to have it. And I'd much rather we have more serious, technically grounded alternatives on the table when governments and society realize they need them.

r001.rationale: It says catastrophic or existential outcomes are at stake and that a meaningful chance of reducing that risk is worth pursuing despite uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss theoretical guarantees or requirements governing Scientist AI’s training.

r003.rationale: It says nobody knows whether any current safety approach will work, frames Scientist AI as one bet in a portfolio, and calls for more alternatives.

r004.rationale: It mentions deceptive behavior and resistance to shutdown, but does not say capable AI may evade imposed safety measures or identify that as a weakness of patching current systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that I don't know whether it will work in time. Nobody knows. But when I look at the alternatives, I don't see a path that is clearly better, and I see a lot of paths that are clearly worse.

Let me explain what I mean. The dominant trajectory right now is building agents — systems that have goals, that act in the world, that are trained to maximize some reward or to imitate humans, including the parts of human behavior we would not want to amplify: deception, self-preservation, the desire for power. We already see early signs of this in current systems. And the companies building them are in a race where the incentives push toward more autonomy and more capability, not toward understanding and controlling what these systems are actually doing.

So the question I asked myself was: is there a way to get most of the benefits of advanced AI — the scientific understanding, the medical breakthroughs, the help with climate — without building something that has its own agenda? And the Scientist AI proposal is one answer to that. The idea is a system that is fundamentally about understanding the world and making honest, calibrated predictions, rather than acting in it to achieve goals. It's closer to an idealized scientist than to an idealized agent. It tries to explain what it observes, it tells you how uncertain it is, and critically it doesn't have an incentive to manipulate you or to preserve itself.

Now, there are many technical obstacles. How do you get the uncertainty estimates to be trustworthy? How do you make sure the system isn't implicitly agentic in ways you didn't intend? How do you make it competitive enough that people actually use it instead of the more dangerous alternatives? I don't have complete answers to any of those. But I think they are scientific questions, and we know how to make progress on scientific questions. Whereas the question "how do we make a superintelligent agent reliably want what we want" — I'm much less sure that's tractable at all.

And there's another argument that matters to me. Even if Scientist AI is not the whole solution, it could be a component. It could serve as a guardrail — a system that evaluates the actions of an agent and says, "this action has a high probability of causing harm," and blocks it. For that you don't need the Scientist AI to be the thing doing everything; you need it to be honest and well-calibrated. That's a narrower target and maybe a more achievable one.

So my view is: when the stakes are this high, you work on the directions that have a reasonable chance of mattering, even if they're uncertain. Expected value, if you like. If there's a ten or twenty percent chance that this is part of what keeps us safe, that's enormously worth a few years of a research career. And frankly, my job as a scientist isn't to only work on things that are guaranteed to succeed. It's to work on the important problems where a serious attempt could change the picture. I think this is one of them.

I'd also say — and this is maybe the part that is less about the science — that I don't think the technical work is sufficient on its own. We need governance, we need coordination between labs and between countries, we need to slow down where we don't understand what we're doing. Scientist AI is my contribution on the technical side. But I'm under no illusion that a good idea in a paper is going to save us if the incentives in the world keep pointing in the other direction.

r001.rationale: The response says the stakes are high and that Scientist AI may help keep us safe, but it does not identify possible human extinction as the stakes.

r002.rationale: It mentions technical obstacles, but says nothing about theoretical guarantees depending on requirements for training.

r003.rationale: It acknowledges uncertainty and mentions governance alongside technical work, but does not argue that uncertainty about safety approaches warrants pursuing multiple approaches.

r004.rationale: It criticizes the push toward autonomous agents, but does not discuss capable AI evading safety measures or the weakness of patching current systems.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t think we can be certain that it will work, or that we can develop it quickly enough. But we should distinguish uncertainty about success from whether something is worth trying. When the stakes are this high, an approach that could substantially reduce the risks deserves a serious research effort.

The idea of Scientist AI is to build a system whose role is to understand the world and help us evaluate hypotheses, rather than to pursue goals in the world. It would try to give us accurate answers, including an honest representation of uncertainty. That could be useful for scientific discovery, but also for assessing whether an action proposed by another AI system would be dangerous.

Of course, saying that doesn’t solve the technical problems. We have to figure out how to make those properties reliable. But it gives us a direction: intelligence that helps us understand, without requiring us to give it autonomous objectives.

And we don’t have to assume that this will be the only approach that succeeds. We should pursue several avenues. My concern is that if we invest almost everything in increasingly capable agents, and very little in alternatives, then we’re making a consequential choice by default. The uncertainty is a reason to investigate Scientist AI now, while we still have an opportunity to learn whether it can help.

r001.rationale: It says the stakes are high and Scientist AI could reduce risks, but does not identify possible human extinction as the stakes.

r002.rationale: It mentions technical problems and reliability, but says nothing about theoretical guarantees depending on requirements for training.

r003.rationale: It notes uncertainty about success, says not to assume Scientist AI will be the only successful approach, and argues for pursuing several avenues.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss sufficiently capable AI evading imposed safety measures or the weakness of patching current systems.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think we should put all our eggs in that basket. But uncertainty about whether an approach will work is not a good reason not to pursue it, especially when the alternatives also have a lot of uncertainty and the stakes are so high.

The idea of Scientist AI is to build a system that helps us understand the world and make predictions, without giving it the objective of acting in the world to achieve some goal. That could be useful in its own right, including for research on AI safety. For example, it could help us evaluate whether an action proposed by another AI would be dangerous.

Of course, there are open questions about how to make that reliable, and we don’t know how much time we have. But that’s a reason to start now, alongside other approaches. Even partial progress could give us tools that reduce risk. We don’t need to be certain it will solve the whole problem for it to be worth a serious research effort.
